title: Call this a hot summer? This phenomenon explains why next year may be worse
gist: A record-speed El Niño declared in June 2026 is developing outside the envelope of anything previously observed — 2.1°C Eastern Pacific anomaly by 30th July versus 1.6°C in 1997 and 1.3°C in 2015 — and is expected to peak later in 2026 with impacts landing in 2027, layering onto oceans already absorbing 23 zettajoules a year. The transmission channels flagged are food prices (ECB: elevated for up to two years), fertiliser (already +35 per cent on the Hormuz shutdown) and sub-Saharan Africa's lost aid buffer.

insights.claim: Mid-July wildfires across France, Spain and Portugal forced more than 300,000 people to evacuate, with Macron calling it the toughest situation since the Second World War.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Establishes a new severity baseline for European insured catastrophe losses that 2027 is forecast to exceed.
insights.locator: Wildfires tore through France, Spain and Portugal

insights.claim: The Bordeaux blaze burned more than 420 square kilometres — roughly four times the size of Paris — ravaged France's famous wine region and came within 15km of the city itself.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Direct physical-asset risk to Bordeaux vineyard and wine-inventory exposure, and to regional reinsurance pricing.
insights.locator: The blaze ravaged France’s famous wine region

insights.claim: The smoke plumes became rare pyrocumulonimbus clouds capable of generating their own lightning and thereby sparking new fires — a self-reinforcing fire mechanism, not a linear one.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Fire loss models built on linear spread assumptions understate tail severity once pyroCb forms.
insights.locator: The giant smoke clouds, such as the one

insights.claim: The UK and Spanish governments jointly declared on 29th July that climate change is now a national security emergency facing Europe, moving climate from environmental to security policy framing.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Security framing unlocks different budget lines and procurement — watch defence-adjacent resilience and civil-protection spending.
insights.quote: this summer’s wildfires demonstrated that climate change was now a national security emergency facing Europe and threatening our way of life.
insights.locator: On 29th July, the British and Spanish governments

insights.claim: Heat records fell far outside Europe too: Salta, Argentina recorded its hottest night on record at 26°C on 18th July despite being mid-winter, and Canadian and US wildfires covered a quarter more land than usual with Dust Bowl-like conditions returning in parts of America.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Simultaneous multi-hemisphere heat stress means agricultural hedges assuming geographic diversification are less effective.
insights.locator: The heat was felt elsewhere, too

insights.claim: El Niño and La Niña are Pacific equatorial warm/cold water cycles that reverse every two to seven years; under neutral or La Niña conditions trade winds push warm water west while cold water wells up in the east, driving the Walker Circulation.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: The reusable mechanism for forecasting which regions get drought versus flood — the input to any ENSO-linked commodity trade.
insights.locator: El Niño and La Niña events are cycles

insights.claim: An El Niño is declared when the Walker Circulation breaks down, trade winds stop and warm subsurface Kelvin waves push east toward South America — which happened in June 2026.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Dates the onset: June 2026, meaning peak effects land in the second half of 2026 and impacts in 2027.
insights.locator: Every two to seven years, El Niño reverses the flow

insights.claim: Last year was only the third warmest on record and may have been held artificially 'cool' by La Niña, meaning the recent temperature series understates the underlying warming trend now that the suppressant has flipped.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Base-rate warning: extrapolating 2025 climate impacts forward materially underprices 2027 risk.
insights.locator: Despite last year being the third warmest year on record

insights.claim: The oceans have absorbed 90 per cent of all heat generated by anthropogenic climate change and now take up 23 zettajoules a year, up from 15 zettajoules as recently as 2021 — a roughly 53 per cent increase in five years.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: The acceleration in ocean heat uptake, not the level, is the signal — it means the El Niño amplifier is loaded far hotter than in any prior cycle.
insights.locator: Our oceans have already absorbed 90 per cent

insights.claim: June 2026 was the warmest ever measured for the world's oceans at 1.17°C above the pre-industrial baseline, with temperatures off southern France and western Italy running 6°C above average.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Mediterranean SST anomalies of that scale precede extreme convective rainfall and flood losses in southern Europe.
insights.locator: No wonder this June was the warmest ever measured

insights.claim: The core question is what a very strong El Niño does when it arrives on top of an already saturated ocean heat sink — a combination for which there is no historical analogue.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Explicitly an out-of-sample event: historical ENSO regressions used in commodity and insurance models have no valid training data.
insights.locator: But what happens when a very strong one arrives

insights.claim: By 30th July the Eastern Pacific anomaly had reached 2.1°C, already crossing the 'super El Niño' threshold well before peak, versus 1.6°C in 1997 and 1.3°C in 2015 on the same date — the two strongest satellite-era events.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: The single hardest number in the piece: this event is running 30-60 per cent hotter than the two prior records at the same calendar point.
insights.quote: No prior year in the 45-year record has been anywhere near this warm this early.
insights.locator: Typically, a sustained 0.5°C rise in temperatures

insights.claim: Berkeley Earth's Zeke Hausfather says this El Niño is set to surpass previous records by a truly mind-blowing margin and that models are forecasting something outside the envelope of anything ever observed, developing faster than the 1997-98 benchmark.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A named IPCC-author forecast of an out-of-distribution event — the credible anchor for positioning ahead of 2027.
insights.quote: The models are forecasting something outside the envelope of anything we have ever observed… The 2026 event is developing faster than 1997-98, the previous gold standard for explosive El Niño onsets,
insights.locator: As Hausfather wrote in mid-July

insights.claim: Hausfather warns that the second half of 2026 and 2027 will be extraordinary for global temperatures on the back of a record-smashing El Niño event, implying the market has not yet absorbed the scale.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Explicit claim that awareness lags reality — the definition of a mispriced risk window.
insights.quote: I’m not sure folks have realized just how crazy the second half of 2026 and 2027 will be for global temperatures—on the back of a record-smashing El Niño event.
insights.locator: This El Niño is set to surpass previous records

insights.claim: UCL's Bill McGuire calls it a 'hyper El Niño' building rapidly and set to bring extreme weather mayhem and record-shattering global temperatures in 2027.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Second independent expert converging on 2027 as the impact year, not 2026.
insights.quote: what I have taken to calling a hyper El Niño is building rapidly, and set to bring extreme weather mayhem and record-shattering global temperatures in 2027.
insights.locator: “Make no mistake”, writes Bill McGuire

insights.claim: Even the normally sober Met Office forecasts a temporary spike in global annual temperature with residual heat potentially making 2027 the hottest year in the series back to 1850 — meaning institutional forecasters, not just outspoken scientists, are aligned.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Consensus among conservative official forecasters removes the 'outlier alarmism' discount from the 2027 thesis.
insights.quote: El Niño will cause a temporary spike in global annual temperature with the residual heat potentially making next year the hottest in the global series from 1850
insights.locator: Even the normally sober Met Office predicts

insights.claim: The European Central Bank finds that a strong El Niño raises global food prices for as long as two years, giving a central-bank-sanctioned transmission channel from ENSO to CPI.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Food inflation persistence into 2028 is a live upside risk to headline CPI paths and therefore to rate-cut expectations.
insights.quote: The European Central Bank finds that a strong El Niño raises global food prices for as long as two years.
insights.locator: A House of Commons Research Briefing

insights.claim: The World Bank warns sub-Saharan Africa is the most exposed region because international aid cuts — specifically the Trump-Musk dismantling of USAID — mean nothing is now saved to cushion a bad harvest.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Removed fiscal buffers convert a weather shock into a sovereign-stress and migration event; watch frontier African credit.
insights.quote: sub-Saharan Africa is the most exposed, with nothing now saved to cushion a bad harvest
insights.locator: While, on the back of international aid cuts

insights.claim: Fertiliser prices jumped 35 per cent in 2026 due to Trump's war with Iran and the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz, compounding the coming harvest shock before El Niño even peaks.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Input-cost inflation and weather shock are stacking in the same crop year — the setup for a genuine agricultural squeeze.
insights.quote: the price of fertiliser also jumped 35 per cent this year due to Trump’s war with Iran and the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz
insights.locator: To make things worse

insights.claim: A House of Commons Research Briefing published in June asked what a 'Godzilla' El Niño means for the UK and answered: likely extreme weather in 2027 and risks to food security.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: UK policy machinery is already scenario-planning for 2027 food security — a tell for forthcoming intervention.
insights.quote: What might a ‘Godzilla’ El Niño mean for the UK?
insights.locator: A House of Commons Research Briefing

insights.claim: The compounding claim is that El Niño arrives into not just hot oceans but a hot mess of geopolitics — the shock lands on a system with its shock absorbers already removed.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Correlation regime shift: weather, energy and aid shocks are no longer independent risks to be diversified across.
insights.quote: El Niño arrives finding not just hot oceans, but also a hot mess of geopolitics.
insights.locator: To make things worse

themes.theme: Tail risk and the long baseline

insights.claim: The 1877 El Niño has been described as arguably the worst environmental disaster ever to befall humanity, instigating famines that killed 3 per cent of the world's population — the historical upper bound for what this cycle can do.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Anchors the tail: ENSO events have historically been civilisation-scale mortality events, not merely commodity price disturbances.
insights.locator: El Niño varies, with weak years and strong years

insights.claim: A 2025 Nature paper warns super El Niño events may provoke persistent or even irreversible changes in the Earth system, including abrupt transition from a quasi-stable ice shelf front to catastrophic large-scale disintegration and sea-level rise.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A low-probability, non-linear pathway from a two-year weather cycle to permanent coastal-asset repricing.
insights.quote: super El Niño events may also provoke persistent or even irreversible changes in other components of the climate and Earth system
insights.locator: A 2025 Nature paper suggests

insights.claim: Bordeaux's maximum June temperature is nearly 6°C higher than 50 years ago, and the region has already recorded more days above 40°C in 2026 than in the entire 105 years since observations began.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Regional viticulture and land values face a step-change, not a drift — the 105-year record was beaten in a single season.
insights.locator: Bordeaux’s maximum June temperature

insights.claim: The closing thesis is that 2026's record-burning summer will likely rank among the coolest summers of the rest of our lives — reframing the current extreme as the new floor rather than the new ceiling.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: If correct, every climate-loss model calibrated on the last decade is anchored to a floor, not a mean.
insights.quote: The truth is that this year’s long, hot, dry, burning summer will likely be one of the coolest summers we have for the rest of our lives.
insights.locator: So, enjoy what’s left of this summer
